#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Secret & Sensitive Data Hygiene Scanner (PRINCIPLE-019)

Secret leakage is the one defect class with no clean rollback: once a credential is pushed,
logged, or sent to a third party, it must be rotated, not reverted. This scanner is therefore a
*pre*-commit gate, the fourth leg of the PRINCIPLE-018 Rule 3 delivery triad.

It scans two surfaces that AI agents leak through in practice:

  1. Staged content (`git diff --cached`), or named files, or the whole tracked tree.
  2. Agent working memory - `.agents/task_ledger.json` free-text fields and the dogfood log.
     This repository's own PRINCIPLE-007 workflow persists `--why` / `--benefits` / `--risks` /
     `--mitigation` straight into a git-tracked ledger, so an agent that quotes a key while
     explaining its reasoning commits that key to history permanently.

Detection is pattern-first (known credential shapes have near-zero false-positive rates) with a
conservative high-entropy fallback for assignment-shaped lines only. Deliberate exceptions use an
inline `# aikit:allow-secret` pragma or the ALLOWLIST_SUBSTRINGS set - never a silenced scanner.

Zero external dependencies (standard library only).

Usage:
  python scripts/check_secrets.py [--staged | --all | --file <path> | --commits <range>] [--verbose]
Exit codes:
  0 clean    1 potential secret found    2 CLI argument misuse
"""

import math
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Tuple

ROOT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
# Agent working memory, relative to the scanned repository: AIKit's ledger and dogfood log, or a
# project's `.aikit/` ledger (ADR-121). Whichever exist are scanned.
AGENT_MEMORY_PATHS = (
    Path(".agents") / "task_ledger.json",
    Path(".agents") / "dogfood_last_run.log",
    Path(".aikit") / "task_ledger.json",
)

PRAGMA = "aikit:allow-secret"
PROC_TIMEOUT = 15

# Known credential shapes. Pattern-first detection keeps false positives near zero, which is what
# keeps the gate trusted; an untrusted gate gets bypassed and protects nothing.
SECRET_PATTERNS: Tuple[Tuple[str, str], ...] = (
    ("AWS access key id", r"\b(?:AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b"),
    ("GitHub token", r"\bgh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{36,}\b"),
    ("GitHub fine-grained token", r"\bgithub_pat_[A-Za-z0-9_]{22,}\b"),
    ("Slack token", r"\bxox[abprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}\b"),
    ("Google API key", r"\bAIza[0-9A-Za-z_\-]{35}\b"),
    # The newer Google AI Studio key format (`AQ.` + 50 chars): a bare one has no key name for the
    # entropy rule to catch (ADR-132).
    ("Google AI Studio key", r"\bAQ\.[0-9A-Za-z_\-]{30,}"),
    ("Stripe secret key", r"\b(?:sk|rk)_(?:live|test)_[0-9A-Za-z]{20,}\b"),
    ("OpenAI-style API key", r"\bsk-(?:proj-)?[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{32,}\b"),

    ("JSON Web Token", r"\beyJ[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}\b"),
    ("Private key block", r"-----BEGIN (?:RSA |EC |OPENSSH |PGP |DSA )?PRIVATE KEY-----"),
    ("Password in URL", r"\b[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.\-]*://[^/\s:@]+:[^/\s:@]+@"),
    ("Authorization header value", r"\bAuthorization\s*[:=]\s*[\"']?(?:Bearer|Basic)\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-=/+]{16,}"),
    ("Hardcoded password assignment", r"\b(?:password|passwd|secret|api_key|apikey|access_token|auth_token|private_key)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{8,}[\"']"),
)

# A value that is wholly an interpolation or a template placeholder is an indirection, not a
# literal credential. This must be honoured by the pattern detectors too, not only the entropy
# fallback: `password = "${DB_PASS}"` is correct code, and a scanner that blocks correct code  # aikit:allow-secret
# gets bypassed, which protects nothing.
INTERPOLATION_ONLY_RE = re.compile(
    r"""[:=]\s*["']?\s*(?:\$\{[^}]*\}|\$[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*|\{\{[^}]*\}\}|"""
    r"""\{[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\}|%\([^)]*\)s|<[^>]*>)\s*["']?\s*$"""
)

# Assignment-shaped lines whose value may be a raw secret; entropy is only applied here.
ASSIGNMENT_RE = re.compile(
    r"(?i)\b([A-Z0-9_]*(?:KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD|PASSWD|CREDENTIAL|AUTH)[A-Z0-9_]*)\s*[:=]\s*[\"']?([^\s\"',;]{16,})[\"']?"
)
# A unified-diff hunk header; group 1 is the first line number on the new side.
HUNK_RE = re.compile(r"^@@ -\d+(?:,\d+)? \+(\d+)(?:,\d+)? @@")
# A quoted token long enough to be a generated key; `looks_random` decides whether it is one.
BARE_LITERAL_RE = re.compile(r"[\"']([A-Za-z0-9_\-]{40,})[\"']")

# Allowlisting is risk-tiered, because a weak word must never veto a high-confidence match.
# A red-check caught this: "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE" was missed purely because the line contained  # aikit:allow-secret
# the word "example", which would equally have hidden a live key on an "# example usage" line.
#
# STRONG markers are unambiguous placeholders and the explicit pragma: they suppress everything.
# WEAK markers suppress only the low-confidence entropy fallback, never a pattern match.
STRONG_ALLOWLIST = frozenset({
    PRAGMA, "your-key-here", "your_key_here", "<your", "placeholder", "changeme",
    "redacted", "<redacted>", "xxxxxxxx", "0000000000",
})
WEAK_ALLOWLIST = frozenset({"example", "sample", "dummy", "fake", "test-token"})

# Retained for callers and tests that want the full token set.
ALLOWLIST_SUBSTRINGS = STRONG_ALLOWLIST | WEAK_ALLOWLIST

# Only the scanner's own pattern table is exempt. Documentation and instruction files can carry a
# pasted credential, so skipping them made `--all`'s "every tracked file" claim false (ADR-163).
SKIP_PATH_PARTS = ("scripts/check_secrets.py",)

TEXT_SUFFIXES = frozenset({
    ".py", ".md", ".txt", ".json", ".yml", ".yaml", ".toml", ".cfg", ".ini", ".env",
    ".sh", ".ps1", ".js", ".ts", ".rs", ".go", ".java", ".rb", ".log", "",
})

def scan_agent_memory(gaps: Optional[List[str]] = None,
                      repo: Path = ROOT_DIR) -> List[Tuple[str, int, str, str]]:
    """
    PRINCIPLE-019 Rule 3: agent working memory is tracked output. The ledger's free-text impact
    fields are committed, so a credential quoted while explaining reasoning becomes permanent.
    """
    findings = []
    for path in (repo / rel for rel in AGENT_MEMORY_PATHS):
        if not path.exists():
            continue
        try:
            findings.extend(scan_text(f"agent-memory:{path.name}",
                                      path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")))
        except OSError as e:
            if gaps is not None:
                gaps.append(f"agent memory {path.name} could not be read: {e}")
    return findings

SCRUB_PLACEHOLDER = "[REDACTED]"


def scrub_text(text: str) -> Tuple[str, List[str]]:
    """
    `text` with every credential-shaped span replaced by `[REDACTED]`, and the detectors hit.

    Used at the boundaries that write free text into tracked state, because PRINCIPLE-019 R5
    makes a leaked credential unrecoverable: refusing or scrubbing the write is worth more than
    reporting it afterwards. Only `SECRET_PATTERNS` run here, never the entropy fallback -
    prose legitimately carries commit hashes and digests, and a scrubber that ate them would be
    worked around rather than fixed (ADR-173). The placeholder is in `STRONG_ALLOWLIST`, so
    scrubbed text is clean when the scanner reads it back.
    """
    detectors: List[str] = []
    scrubbed = text
    for detector, pattern in SECRET_PATTERNS:
        scrubbed, hits = re.subn(pattern, SCRUB_PLACEHOLDER, scrubbed)
        if hits:
            detectors.append(detector)
    return scrubbed, detectors

cat >> knowledge/decisions.md <<'ADR'


### ADR-173: Credentials Are Refused or Scrubbed at the Write Boundary
- **Date**: 2026-10-22
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: PRINCIPLE-019 R5 makes a leaked credential the one defect with no clean rollback: it must be rotated, never reverted. `check_secrets.py` already treated the task ledger and the dogfood log as scanning surfaces under R3, because this repository's own PRINCIPLE-007 workflow writes `--why`, `--benefits`, `--risks` and `--mitigation` straight into a git-tracked file. But the scanner only reported after the text was already on disk, and in a pre-commit gate that means the value is in the working tree and one `git add` away from permanence. Its pattern table also covered 15 shapes and missed common prefixed formats. Separately, a sub-agent's answer reaches the lead agent's context and anything that logs it, with no scanning surface at all.
- **Decision**:
  1. `SECRET_PATTERNS` gains 13 shapes — GitLab, npm, PyPI, SendGrid, Hugging Face, Google OAuth client secret, Mailgun, Telegram bot, Docker Hub, Notion, Linear, Slack incoming webhook and Azure storage account key — and the private-key block recognizes `ENCRYPTED` and `SSH2 ENCRYPTED` headers. Every addition is anchored on a literal vendor prefix. No bare-length pattern and no PII pattern is added.
  2. `scrub_text(text)` returns the text with each credential-shaped span replaced by `[REDACTED]` plus the detectors that fired. It runs `SECRET_PATTERNS` only, never the entropy fallback or the bare-literal rule, because prose legitimately carries commit hashes and digests. `[REDACTED]` is already in `STRONG_ALLOWLIST`, so scrubbed text is clean when the scanner reads it back.
  3. `checkpoint_command` — the one path both `disruption_recovery.py --checkpoint` and `aikit checkpoint` take (ADR-128) — checks the description and the four impact fields before it reads or writes the ledger. A hit exits 1 and names the detector, the rule and `--redact`. With `--redact` the scrubbed text is recorded instead, and the PRINCIPLE-007 R6 impact validation then runs against the text that will actually be written.
  4. `answer_text` scrubs the sub-agent's answer unconditionally. There is no opt-in, because no caller wants a leaked key verbatim and nothing is lost by redacting one.
  5. `disruption_recovery.py` imports `scrub_text` through both `scripts.check_secrets` and `check_secrets`. It is the only directly-runnable script in the repository with a local import, and every other one is a standalone leaf; the two-form import keeps `python scripts/disruption_recovery.py` working, where only `scripts/` is on `sys.path`, without a `sys.path` bootstrap. If both forms fail the `ImportError` propagates.
- **Consequences**:
  - *Positive*: A credential quoted in an impact note is refused before it reaches a tracked file instead of being found afterwards, which is the only point at which PRINCIPLE-019 R5 can still be satisfied cheaply. Sub-agent output cannot carry a key into the lead agent's context. The pattern table nearly doubles, to 28 shapes, while keeping the near-zero false-positive property the gate's trust depends on; a regression test asserts a risk note citing a commit hash and a `sha256:` digest still scans clean.
  - *Trade-offs*: `--checkpoint` gains a refusal path, so a script that writes credential-shaped free text now exits 1 where it used to succeed. Patterns that include the key name, such as the hardcoded-password assignment, scrub the name along with the value, so `password = "..."` becomes `[REDACTED]` rather than `password = "[REDACTED]"` — safe, but it loses the field name from the note. `--redact` records that a credential was present without recording which value, so the operator still has to rotate it; the Fix line says so explicitly. The two-form import is a deliberate exception to the standalone-leaf rule and is the first local import in the module every other script imports from; `--help` measured 164 ms against the 200 ms budget, so a further import there would need re-measuring.
  - *Limitation*: Pattern detection cannot catch a credential that does not look like one. A short memorable password, an internal hostname or a bare opaque token with no vendor prefix still passes, and the entropy fallback that might catch some of them is deliberately not applied to prose.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The mechanisms serve PRINCIPLE-003 R3 (standard library only; no new dependency), PRINCIPLE-005 R2 (README documents the flag in the same commit), PRINCIPLE-009 R5 (the new import adds no cycle; the gate lives in the one shared path), PRINCIPLE-010 (the `--help` budget re-measured), PRINCIPLE-011 R1 and R5 (standalone invocation preserved; exit 1 for an operational failure), PRINCIPLE-013 (the refusal precedes the lock and the write, so no partial state is possible), PRINCIPLE-014 R1 (a failing-first test per pattern and per wiring point) and PRINCIPLE-019 R3, R4 and R5.
ADR

Item 2 done — `8604ef0`, verified in isolation, clean tree.

**What shipped**

The scanner went from 15 to 28 credential shapes (GitLab, npm, PyPI, SendGrid, Hugging Face, Google OAuth, Mailgun, Telegram, Docker Hub, Notion, Linear, Slack webhooks, Azure account keys, plus `ENCRYPTED`/`SSH2` private-key headers). All vendor-prefixed — I deliberately added no bare-length or PII patterns, because the file's own design comment is right that a scanner which blocks correct code gets bypassed.

More importantly, detection moved **before** the write. `checkpoint_command` is the single path both `--checkpoint` and `aikit checkpoint` take, so one change covers both: a credential shape in the description or any impact field now exits 1 and names `--redact`, *before* the ledger is read or written. `--redact` records `[REDACTED]` instead. Sub-agent output is scrubbed unconditionally. A regression test pins that a risk note citing a commit hash and a `sha256:` digest still scans clean.

**Three things worth knowing**

**I broke standalone invocation and caught it.** Importing `check_secrets` into `disruption_recovery` worked under `unittest` but broke `python scripts/disruption_recovery.py --help` — every directly-runnable script here is deliberately a standalone leaf, and CI asserts that `--help` exits 0. Fixed with a documented two-form import rather than a `sys.path` bootstrap. `--help` now measures 145 ms against the 200 ms budget; a further import there would need re-measuring.

**A trade-off I'd flag rather than bury.** Patterns that include the key name scrub the name too — `password = "..."` becomes `[REDACTED]`, not `password = "[REDACTED]"`. Safe, but a redacted note loses which field leaked. ADR-173 records it, along with the real limitation: pattern detection cannot catch a credential that doesn't look like one, and the entropy fallback is deliberately not applied to prose.

**The README ceiling hit, one item early.** My first draft of the documentation put the file at 22,504 of 22,500 — the gate failed. I tightened my own clause rather than cutting your prose, and it now sits at **22,485: 15 characters left**.

def quick_reference_errors(readme: str) -> List[str]:
    """
    The structure PRINCIPLE-005 R1 states, not just its words: a heading, then inside its section
    a `- **Runtime Prerequisites**:` line naming a version and a fenced command right after the
    test-gate label. A substring check passed a README that merely mentioned the labels in prose.
    """
    heading = re.search(r"^(#{1,6}) [^\n]*Cold-Start Quick Reference", readme, re.M)
    if not heading:
        return ["README.md has no heading containing 'Cold-Start Quick Reference' (R1)"]
    rest = readme[heading.end():]
    following = re.search(rf"^#{{1,{len(heading.group(1))}}} ", rest, re.M)
    section = rest[:following.start()] if following else rest
    errors: List[str] = []
    prerequisites = re.search(r"^- \*\*Runtime Prerequisites\*\*:([^\n]*)", section, re.M)
    if not prerequisites:
        errors.append("the Quick Reference has no line starting '- **Runtime Prerequisites**:' (R1)")
    elif not re.search(r"\d", prerequisites.group(1)):
        errors.append("'- **Runtime Prerequisites**:' names no minimum version (R1)")
    if not re.search(r"\*\*Canonical Regression Shield Gate\*\*:[ \t]*\n[ \t]*```[^\n]*\n[ \t]*\S", section):
        errors.append("the Quick Reference has no fenced command right after "
                      "'**Canonical Regression Shield Gate**:' (R1)")
    return errors

## What I found

README composition, measured:

| Section | Chars | Editable? |
|---|---|---|
| Principle tables | 5,731 (25.5%) | **No** — generated by `sync_principles.py` from the capsules, which have 0–4 chars of slack |

| "Start a Project" | 3,864 | Free prose |
| Everything else | 3,466 | Free prose |

A quarter of the file is off limits, and five command strings are frozen verbatim by `test_workflow_commands_match_documented_commands`.

## What I changed — 298 chars, zero words

The tree aligned its `<-` comments at **column 40**, driven by a single 39-character entry while most entries are under 25. That's **930 characters of pure padding**. I plotted the trade-off:

```
column 36:  208 saved,  1 entry overflows
column 34:  309 saved,  3 entries overflow
column 30:  498 saved,  9 entries overflow
column 26:  655 saved, 17 entries overflow
```

Column 36 is the knee — 208 chars for one line losing alignment. Plus a stray blank line inside the tree that broke the `│` spine between `scripts/` and `tests/`, two runs of double blank lines, and padding in hand-written table cells.

**Verified rather than asserted:** comparing the word sequence against HEAD with the table pipe treated as a separator — **2,826 words, identical and in the same order.** Headroom: **15 → 313**.

Two things worth knowing:

**The unit tier caught me overreaching.** My first pass stripped padding from *all* table cells, including the generated principle table, so `sync_readme_table` no longer reproduced the file and two tests failed. Regenerating restored the generator's own spacing — which cost 75 of the 373 chars I'd initially recovered. That's the right outcome: the generated region isn't mine to reformat.

**Entries can't be merged, only shortened.** `audit_readme` parses one path per tree line and requires every tracked entry to appear, so combining `CLAUDE.md / GEMINI.md` onto one line would fail the gate. Worth knowing before anyone tries it.

Roughly **120 more characters** from genuine redundancy, which I did *not* touch because it changes wording and you asked for no meaning loss:

- Synonym triples in the `knowledge/` tree comments — "Data structures, schemas, and persistence models", "Presentation layer, UI state, and event loops", "Knowledge base table of contents & architecture map" (~90 chars)
- `Read-only;` on two matrix rows, already stated by the Universal CLI contract paragraph below the table (~22 chars)

The `ui` paragraph is ~1,900 characters in one sentence chain and is the only place with real structural slack, but condensing it is a rewrite with actual meaning risk. I'd leave it unless the budget forces the issue.

**313 characters is enough for items 3 and 4** without touching prose, so I'd stop here. One useful property: if a future edit re-aligns the tree to column 40, `update_knowledge_base.py --check` fails on size — the regression is self-detecting rather than silent.

    """
    lines = [
        "============================================================",
        "⚡ DISRUPTION RESUMPTION GUIDANCE (PRINCIPLE-006)",
        "============================================================",
    ]
    lines += audit_body_lines(audit)
    if audit.get("conflicted_files"):
        lines.append("⛔ BLOCKED: resolve the conflicts above before any other action.")

    if audit.get("ledger_error"):
        lines.append("⛔ BLOCKED: this ledger cannot be read by this AIKit; no task state was changed.")
        lines.append("============================================================")
        return "\n".join(lines)

    interrupted = audit.get("interrupted_task")
    if not interrupted:
        if audit.get("modified_files") or audit.get("untracked_files") or audit.get("dangling_temp_files"):
            lines.append("🟡 No interrupted task, but the files above are uncommitted: inspect them before a new task and never overwrite them.")
        elif not audit.get("conflicted_files"):
            lines.append("🟢 No interrupted task detected. Ready for a new task.")
        lines.append("============================================================")
        return "\n".join(lines)

    task_id = interrupted.get("task_id", "unknown")
    phase = interrupted.get("last_phase", "unknown")
    phase_num = resolve_active_phase(interrupted, default=2)
    # PRINCIPLE-002 R4 records a checkpoint on ENTERING a phase, so the recorded phase is the one
    # in progress: resume there. Guessing "phase + 1" when the tree was clean skipped work - after
    # a PRINCIPLE-006 milestone commit during Phase 3, it sent the agent straight to Phase 4.
    next_phase_num = phase_num
    
    lines.append(f"⚠️  RESUMING INTERRUPTED TASK: '{task_id}'")
    lines.append(f"📌 Last Active Phase: Phase {phase_num} ({phase})")
    lines.append(f"🚀 Recommended Resumption Phase: Phase {next_phase_num}")
    if audit.get("plan"):
        lines.append(f"🗺️  Plan (Phase 2 checkpoint): {audit['plan']}")
    if audit.get("dangling_temp_files"):
        lines.append(f"🧹 Action Needed: Purge {len(audit['dangling_temp_files'])} dangling .tmp_* files (run 'python scripts/disruption_recovery.py --clean')")
    lines.append(f"💡 Next Action: Inspect surviving files, run unit tests, and resume at Phase {next_phase_num}")
    lines.append("============================================================")
    return "\n".join(lines)

RISK_DIMENSIONS = ("contract:", "dependency:", "concurrency:", "state:")

# The handoff packet (PRINCIPLE-004 R2, ADR-174). `--resume` already prints the plan; these are
# the things it could not know: progress against that plan, a dead end not worth retrying, a
# question still owed to the user, and what has already been verified.
HANDOFF_KEYS = ("state", "next", "failed", "open", "evidence")
MAX_HANDOFF_CHARS = 2000


def parse_handoff(text: str) -> Tuple[Dict[str, str], List[str]]:
    """
    One `--handoff` string as `{key: value}`, plus the reasons it is unusable.

    The format is `--risks`' own: `key: value` segments separated by `;`, so an agent that can
    write one can write the other. A value may contain `:` - only the first one in a segment
    separates the key - and empty segments are ignored, so a trailing `;` is not an error.
    """
    if len(text) > MAX_HANDOFF_CHARS:
        return {}, [f"--handoff is {len(text)} characters; the limit is {MAX_HANDOFF_CHARS} "
                    f"so a packet stays readable after a compaction"]
    packet: Dict[str, str] = {}
    errors: List[str] = []
    for segment in text.split(";"):
        if not segment.strip():
            continue
        key, separator, value = segment.partition(":")
        key = key.strip().lower()
        if not separator or key not in HANDOFF_KEYS:
            errors.append(f"--handoff does not know the key '{key or segment.strip()}'; "
                          f"it accepts {', '.join(HANDOFF_KEYS)}")
            continue
        if value.strip():
            packet[key] = value.strip()
    if not errors and "next" not in packet:
        errors.append("--handoff must give a 'next:' value: the one action that resumes this task")
    return packet, errors

cat >> knowledge/decisions.md <<'ADR'


### ADR-174: The Checkpoint Carries a Cold-Start Handoff Packet
- **Date**: 2026-10-22
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: `--resume` prints the plan (PRINCIPLE-004 R1) but nothing about progress against it. Resuming `aikit-scaffold-lint-fixes-v1` this session meant reading a git diff to learn which of its six milestones were already done, because the ledger had no place to say so. Three other things had no home either: an approach already tried and rejected, which a resumed agent is free to repeat; a question put to the user and still unanswered, which a compaction simply erases; and what had already been verified, so Phase 4 is either redone blindly or trusted blindly. `format_resume_report`'s own "Next Action" line was a hardcoded string telling every task to inspect surviving files and run the unit tier, which is the same generic-default defect class `check_reachability.py` was built after.
- **Decision**:
  1. A checkpoint may carry an optional `handoff` object with the keys `next` (required), `state`, `failed`, `open` and `evidence`.
  2. `--handoff` takes one string of `key: value` segments separated by `;`, the format `--risks` already uses, so an agent that can write one can write the other. Only the first `:` in a segment separates the key, so a value may contain colons; empty segments are ignored; an unknown key or a missing `next` exits 2 and names the accepted keys; the input is bounded to 2,000 characters.
  3. **No ledger schema version bump.** `validate_ledger_version` refuses any version that is not exactly `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION`, including an older one, so bumping to 2 would have made AIKit's own ledger and all 20 registered projects' ledgers unreadable. The change is purely additive instead: the key is absent unless given, every reader uses `.get()`, and an older build ignores it harmlessly.
  4. The packet's text passes through the ADR-173 credential gate with the description and the impact fields, so `--handoff` is not a new way to write a credential into a tracked file.
  5. `--resume` prints the latest packet belonging to the active task — an older one describes a state already moved past — and uses its `next` in place of the generic Next Action line. A task with no packet keeps the old line, so nothing is lost for a task that records none.
- **Consequences**:
  - *Positive*: A resumed agent reads what was done, what failed, what is open and what to do next instead of re-deriving it from a diff. An unanswered user question survives compaction. The cold-start Next Action becomes task-specific. One flag and one parser, consistent with an existing validated format.
  - *Trade-offs*: `aikit checkpoint` and `--checkpoint` gain a flag, and `--resume` gains up to four lines of output against PRINCIPLE-004 R5's 100-line budget; a test pins the report inside it. The packet is the agent's own account of its work: unlike a test or a hash, nothing can verify that `failed` or `evidence` is true, so it is a memory aid and never evidence in the PRINCIPLE-014 sense. `next` is required, which makes a packet that only answers "what failed" impossible to record — deliberate, since a packet with no next action does not help a cold start.
  - *Limitation*: Only 20 checkpoints are retained, so a packet older than that window is pruned with its checkpoint. The plan checkpoint is exempt from pruning; a handoff is not.
- **Reported, not fixed here**: `validate_ledger_version` refusing *older* versions contradicts `knowledge/data_models.md`, which states that only a newer version is refused in place. The two have been indistinguishable because the version has only ever been 1. Any future bump that genuinely needs one must fix that first, or every existing ledger becomes unreadable. Left out of this task under PRINCIPLE-007 R4.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The mechanisms serve PRINCIPLE-004 R1, R2 and R5 (the cold-start report, bounded), PRINCIPLE-005 R2 (README documents the flag in the same commit), PRINCIPLE-006 (resumption after disruption), PRINCIPLE-011 R5 (exit 2 for a malformed packet), PRINCIPLE-013 R4 (no schema break; the existing migration is untouched), PRINCIPLE-014 R1 (a failing-first test per behaviour) and PRINCIPLE-016 R5 (the fields are written only to `knowledge/data_models.md`).
ADR

**I was wrong about the schema bump, and it would have been bad.** My proposal said "schema v2 + migration". Reading `validate_ledger_version` first: it refuses **any** version that isn't exactly current, *including older ones*. Bumping to 2 would have made AIKit's own ledger and all 20 registered projects' ledgers unreadable — `--resume`, `--audit`, `aikit status` and `aikit check` would all have failed. The handoff is purely additive, so it needs no bump: the key is absent unless given, every reader uses `.get()`, and an older build ignores it.

**The reachability shield rejected my first implementation, correctly.** I wrote the keys with a comprehension over `HANDOFF_KEYS`, which hides every literal producer, so `handoff['next']` read as a phantom key. Writing them key by key is what makes the shield's guarantee real.

**Two defects found in the gates themselves, reported not fixed** (P-007 R4 — outside this task's plan; both are in ADR-174):

1. `validate_ledger_version` refusing *older* versions contradicts `knowledge/data_models.md`, which says only a newer version is refused in place. They've been indistinguishable because the version has only ever been 1. **Any future bump that genuinely needs one must fix this first**, or every existing ledger breaks.
2. `check_reachability.py:264` — `all_literals` is a `set`, so `sum(1 for lit in all_literals if lit == key)` can never exceed 1. The "a key appearing more than once has a producer" fallback is dead code, and its comment claims behaviour it doesn't have. Direction is safe (false positives, not false negatives), but it makes the gate stricter than documented.

def render_tier1_target(heading: str, principles: List[Dict], domain_rules: str = "") -> str:
    """
    Render one always-injected Tier 1 target (PRINCIPLE-001 R1/R3, PRINCIPLE-017 R2).

    The header deliberately says *when* to read Tier 2, not merely *that* it exists. The former
    "Strictly follow all principles defined in AGENTS.md and GUIDELINES.md" invited agents to
    load ~27k tokens of Tier 2 up front - the exact bloat PRINCIPLE-001 exists to prevent. It also
    marks the file as generated, so a hand edit is not silently overwritten by the next sync.
    """
    lines = [
        heading,
        "",
        # Wording mirrors PRINCIPLE-001 R1 (precedence) and R3 (trigger names) exactly; a test
        # keeps the two in lock-step so every agent receives the same instruction.
        f"> Generated from `{SSOT_MD.name}` by `scripts/sync_principles.py`; do not edit.",
        "> Capsules bind; `GUIDELINES.md` wins on conflict. On a contract change, failure or "
        "ambiguity, read the `### PRINCIPLE-NNN:` section of each principle "
        "`sync_principles.py --involved` lists; never the whole file unless asked.",
        "",
        "## Core Principles",
    ]
    for p in principles:
        label = f"{p['id']} {tier1_title(p['title'])}"
        summary = p.get("invariant") or p.get("concept")
        # Plain labels: bold markers are decoration (PRINCIPLE-001 R7), ~4 chars x every line.
        lines.append(f"- {label}: {summary}")
    lines.append("")
    append_domain_rules(lines, domain_rules)
    return "\n".join(lines)

### ADR-175: The Tier 1 Header Stops Naming Its Own Generator
- **Date**: 2026-10-22
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The Tier 1 context budget is 1,600 estimated tokens per target, and PRINCIPLE-001's headroom rule requires the universal rules to still fit with a full 1,200-character Tier 1B block, so the real limit is 6,403 characters of rendered text. Measured across all eight targets, the worst (`.agents/rules/principles.md`) sat at 6,400: **three characters free**. That blocks any further Tier 1 text, including the `.agents/skills/aikit/SKILL.md` pointer the kit needs because the operational runbook is auto-discovered by only two of the eight supported hosts and no Tier 1 file references it.     """

    Deliberately neither OSError nor ValueError: load_ledger() treats those as corruption and

def locked_ledger(
    ledger_file: Optional[Path] = None,
    timeout_seconds: float = LOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
    poll_interval: float = 0.05,
):
    """
    Serialize a full read-modify-write cycle on the task ledger (PRINCIPLE-013 Rule 3).

    Yields the loaded ledger; the caller mutates it in place and the ledger is saved on clean
    exit, all while holding the advisory lock. Without this, parallel subagents interleave
    load/save cycles and silently erase each other's checkpoints (lost-update race).

    Contention is surfaced, never swallowed: if the lock cannot be acquired within the bounded
    timeout the mutation is abandoned with a diagnostic rather than written unprotected.
    """
    path = Path(ledger_file) if ledger_file is not None else LEDGER_PATH
    with file_lock(path, timeout_seconds=timeout_seconds, poll_interval=poll_interval) as acquired:
        if not acquired:
            raise TimeoutError(
                f"[PRINCIPLE-013 LOCK CONTENTION] Could not acquire advisory lock on "
                f"{path.name} within {timeout_seconds}s. "
                f"Why: another agent or process is mid-write on the ledger. "
                f"Fix: retry shortly, or remove a stale '{path.name}.lock' if no process is active."
            )

def _git_start(project_root: Path) -> None:
    """
    `git init`, then commit the project's memory and instructions so a new project starts clean.
    Raises when the commit cannot be made (typically no git identity): a clean baseline is required
    for delivery and the UI guard, and AIKit never invents an author.
    """
    result = _run_git(project_root, "init", "--quiet")
    if result.returncode != 0:
        raise ProjectError(
            f"`git init` failed in {project_root}: {result.stderr.strip()}",
            "every project is its own git repository, separate from AIKit's.",
            "fix the git error above, then run the command again.",
        )
    stage_items = [".gitignore", "README.md", PROJECT_MEMORY_DIRNAME]
    _run_git(project_root, "add", "--", *stage_items)
    result = _run_git(project_root, "commit", "--quiet", "-m", "chore: start project with AIKit memory")

            "set `git config user.name` and `git config user.email` (or repo-local equivalents), "
            "then run `aikit new` again.",
        )
    return None

content.text:
The other AI's work is substantively **correct and better than mine in four places** — but it shipped one real process violation, and none of the three issues you raised were addressed.

## What it did

1. **Rewrote four of my unpushed commits** (`8604ef0`, `749c1b9`, `278f3f5`, `83f462a` → `53dee30`, `342ca15`, `85e7cbb`, `83b67de`). The only change: credential-shaped test fixtures re-encoded as escape sequences — `glpat-` became `glpat\x2d`. The runtime strings are identical, so behaviour is unchanged. This is almost certainly to get past GitHub push protection, which scans every pushed commit and ignores `# aikit:allow-secret`. Rewriting was the right tool for that: a forward fix wouldn't help, because the literals would still be in earlier commits.
2. **`8216db9`** — five changes in one commit: finished my budget/pointer task, plus four fixes.
3. **`9653975`** — a one-line codebase map fix.
4. **Pushed everything.** Origin moved `b73e148` → `9653975` as a fast-forward. None of my original hashes had ever been published, so nothing shared was overwritten. I never had push authorization; whether it did is for you to say.

## Verification of each change

| Change | Verdict | How I checked |
|---|---|---|
| Budget 1600 → 1750, rule text, the 90% warning recomputed to 1,575 | ✅ Correct | Same as my staged edits; parity test and `sync --check` pass |
| Runbook pointer in all 8 targets | ✅ **Better than mine** | Uses a `RUNBOOK_PATH` constant shared with the `.claude/` mirror; margin now **548 chars** |
| `status --json --exit-code` honours `--exit-code` | ✅ **Fixes my bug** | My JSON branch ignored the flag entirely, so CI got exit 0 on a dirty tree |
| `project_is_clean` includes `ledger_error` | ✅ **Fixes my bug** | Mine printed `"clean": true` while exiting 1 |
| All delegate report paths scrubbed | ✅ **Fixes my bug** | I scrubbed only `answer_text`; `--format json` and the failure path leaked raw stdout/stderr |
| Font token checked in the declaration's value only | ✅ **Fixes my bug** | Old vs new on 6 cases: only change is `font-family: Arial; color: var(--x)`, which I passed and it flags |
| `create_project` warning channel removed | ✅ Correct | Dead since my `e6e708b` made git failures raise; all 6 call sites updated |

Every behaviour fix has a test. Tip is green: 483 tests across 7 runs, all six gates.

I'll be direct: **ADR-172 and ADR-173 overclaimed.** I wrote that the payload and exit code "cannot disagree by construction" and that the sub-agent's answer was scrubbed "unconditionally" — both were true of one path and false of another.

## What it got wrong

**Five pushed commits fail their own gate.** The rewrite changed `test_kit.py`'s bytes without regenerating the codebase map, which records that size. I checked every commit:

```
53dee30  342ca15  85e7cbb  83b67de  8216db9   → STALE map
9653975                                      → ok
```

`83b67de` exits 1 on `update_knowledge_base.py --check` in an isolated worktree, confirmed. That breaks P-018 R7 (each commit verified alone), and `9653975` patches it only at the tip. My originals each passed `verify_commit.py`. The fix would have been regenerating the map inside each rewritten commit. **Since it's published, I'd leave history alone** — the tip is correct, and repairing it would take a force-push.

Minor: bundling five unrelated changes into `fix(review)` cuts against the milestone-per-commit convention.

## Your earlier question — the three claims

The other AI touched none of them; all three are still present.

**`ui finish` message — true, and worse than described.** `finish()` returns the review-missing finding *only* when `verify()` found nothing, so "the UI change is outside its contract" (`aikit_cli.py:650`) is false in exactly the case it fires. The first remedy offered is `ui abort`, which restores the surface to baseline — it **discards valid work**. The JSON code `ui.review-missing` is already correct; only the human text is wrong. Your read is right: the gate is fine, the message is not.

**`check_reachability` dead fallback — true, proven.** `all_literals` is a set, so the count is always 0 or 1, `occurrences <= 1` is always true, and the AST walk feeding it is wasted work.

**`validate_ledger_version` — true, but I overstated it as a defect.** The code refuses anything `!=` current, and `data_models.md` says only *newer* is refused, in two places. But `test_invalid_ledger_versions_are_refused` deliberately pins `0` and `-1` — those are invalid values, not past schemas. The hazard is real but latent: the first genuine bump makes every v1 ledger unreadable, because `migrate_ledger_schema` runs *after* validation and can never upgrade across versions. And the same `!=` is in `save_ledger` at line 478, so there are **two** places to fix, not one.

## Next

1. **`ui finish` message** — say the review is the only blocker and drop the revert/abort advice. Small and clear.
2. **Reachability dead code** — delete it. Behaviour is identical, so it's safe.
3. **Ledger version check** — this one needs your call, since rejecting `0`/`-1` is deliberate. My suggestion: refuse `< 1` or `> current`, and route valid older versions through migration, in both places.

Separately, there are three stale worktrees in Temp and Kilo's pool. They predate my session, so they're unrelated to this review; I can prune them if you want. Shall I do 1 and 2 now?
Does it matter those worktrees? Also verify those findings in the next.

Two things: whether the worktrees matter, and reproducing each "Next" finding concretely rather than by reading code. Both are read-only, so I'll change nothing.

**No, not functionally.** They total about 7 MB. All three are on detached HEADs, so none locks a branch. Every commit they pin is already in `main`'s history, so they keep no extra objects alive. And nothing in `scripts/`, `tests/` or CI ever lists worktrees, so they can't affect a gate.

- **`aikit_verify_2se8ob_r`** (10-21) — left by a `verify_commit.py` run that was hard-killed. Its `finally` cleanup can't run on a kill. Safe to delete.
- **`aikit_baseline_budget`** (10-21) — no AIKit code creates that name, so an agent made it by hand. Safe to delete.
- **Kilo's pool worktree** — owned and managed by Kilo. **Leave it.**

The one real observation is minor: `verify_commit.py` has no startup sweep for leftovers, so each hard kill leaves ~2.7 MB in Temp. I'd only fix that if it keeps happening.

## The three findings, reproduced

**1. `ui finish` message — confirmed end to end.** I ran a real sandbox project through the real CLI, no mocks. On one tree, `ui verify` printed `[OK] UI surface verified`; seconds later `ui finish` printed `Error: the UI change is outside its contract` and told me to "revert the listed paths" when none were listed. The JSON code `ui.review-missing` is already correct; only the human text is wrong.

Correction to my last report: following the advice to run `ui abort` reverted the valid edit and closed the task, but the work is **not destroyed**. `abort` saved the full edit as `changes.patch` in Temp, recoverable with `git apply`. The harm is real but bounded.

**2. Reachability dead code — confirmed, and my recommendation reverses.** A set can only count to 1, so the guard is always true. Two corrections:

- **Cost is negligible.** My first timing (142 ms vs 11 ms) was distorted because the parser caches syntax trees and the guarded version paid for parsing first. Measured fairly, best of five in both orders, it's **17 ms vs 10 ms**.
- **Don't fix it to match its comment.** I rebuilt the handoff bug from this session, where a dict comprehension hid the producer. The current strict shield **flags** it. A version fixed to count as the comment describes **lets it through**, because `next` appears three times as a literal. Fixing it that way would weaken a safety gate. The right fix is to delete the dead code, correct the comment, and add a test so nobody "fixes" it later.

**3. Ledger version — confirmed, and the blast radius is bigger than I said.** I simulated a v2 build against copies of real ledgers:
- Both AIKit's ledger and `tally`'s are refused on read, and `save_ledger` refuses on write.
- `migrate_ledger_schema` is called **0 times**, so the upgrade path can never run.
- There are **27 ledgers, all version 1** — ADR-174's "20 projects" undercounts.
- The refusal leaves files untouched and gives a clear message. The failure mode is every ledger command stopping until the code is fixed, not data loss.

The fix I proposed, `type(v) is not int or v < 1 or v > CURRENT` in both places, still refuses every case the existing test pins (`True`, `"2"`, `2.0`, `0`, `-1`, and newer). With `CURRENT = 1` it behaves exactly as today; it only changes what a future bump does.

**The flaky test.** There was one failure in 13 full runs, and none in the 12 since. I lost its name last time, and I've now shown worktrees can't affect tests, so my guess was wrong. **The cause is unknown.** It isn't traceable to the other AI's changes either.

fix(ui): [milestone 1/3] finish says review is the only blocker

`ui finish` without --reviewed printed "Error: the UI change is
outside its contract", told the user to "revert the listed paths"
(none were listed) and led with `ui abort`. But finish() reports a
missing review only after verify() found nothing, so in exactly that
case the change is inside its contract. Reproduced on a real sandbox
project: `ui verify` printed [OK] and `ui finish` on the same tree
said the opposite; following the advice to run `ui abort` reverted
the valid edit and closed the task (recoverable only from a
changes.patch left in Temp).

When every finding is ui.review-missing, finish now says the change
passed verification and that only the human review is missing, and
gives the one command that closes the task. The branch keys on the
stable finding code, not the message text, so it cannot drift from
the JSON contract. Exit code stays 1 and the JSON output is unchanged;
a real contract finding keeps the full revert/allow/abort advice.

Re-verified on the sandbox after the fix: the new message, exit 1,
then `ui finish --reviewed` closes the task with the edit intact.

Phase 4 on this tree: 485 tests, rule sync, AST map, reachability,
secrets, dogfood. check_test_budgets.py failed once and passed on an
immediate re-run of the unchanged tree; it runs both tiers, which
include dogfood's --help timing track, a pre-existing flake measured
in this session (aikit.py --help has a ~160ms floor under a 200ms
single-sample budget at every revision back to 10-22).

find_phantom_keys had a fallback meant to excuse a key appearing more
than once as a string literal. It collected the literals into a set,
so `sum(1 for lit in all_literals if lit == key)` could only be 0 or
1, `occurrences <= 1` was always true, and the fallback never excused
anything. Its comment described behaviour the code did not have.

Removed rather than repaired. Rebuilding this session's ADR-174 defect
(a producer hidden in a comprehension over a tuple of key names): the
current strict shield flags it; the fallback repaired to count
occurrences would pass it, because the key's name appears three times
as a literal. Making the code match its comment would have weakened a
safety gate.

Behaviour is unchanged, so under PRINCIPLE-014 R1 no failing-first
test applies. A pin is added instead -
test_a_producer_hidden_in_a_comprehension_is_flagged - and
mutation-checked: it passes against this shield and fails against the
repaired counting version. The comment now states the strict rule and
why the fallback must not come back.

Measured cost of the deleted walk: ~7ms (17ms vs 10ms best of five in
both orders; module_nodes caches parsed trees, so an earlier 142ms
reading was cold parsing, not this code).

secrets, test budgets, dogfood. Two of four captured Phase 4 sequences
hit the pre-existing dogfood --help timing flake (aikit.py --help took

def ledger_version_supported(version: Any) -> bool:
    """
    Whether this build can read a ledger declaring `version`: an int from 1 to the current schema.

    An older valid version is supported because `migrate_ledger_schema` upgrades it; only a newer
    one, or a value that is not a real version (`0`, `-1`, `True`, `"1"`, `1.0`), is refused.
    Both the read and the write path ask this one question: the check used to be `!=` in each,
    so the first schema bump would have refused every existing ledger (ADR-178).
    """
    return type(version) is int and 1 <= version <= LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION


def validate_ledger_version(data: Any, path: Path) -> None:
    """Refuse a ledger whose declared schema this build does not read (PRINCIPLE-013 R4)."""
    if not isinstance(data, dict) or "version" not in data:
        return
    version = data.get("version")
    if not ledger_version_supported(version):
        raise UnsupportedLedgerVersion(path, version, LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION)

cat >> knowledge/decisions.md <<'ADR'


### ADR-178: An Older Valid Ledger Version Is Upgraded, Not Refused
- **Date**: 2026-10-23
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: `validate_ledger_version` (read) and `save_ledger` (write) each refused any version that was not exactly `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION`. `knowledge/data_models.md` stated twice that only a *newer* version is refused, and PRINCIPLE-013 R4 refuses only "a version the reader does not support" and routes loaded data through `migrate_ledger_schema`. While the version has only ever been 1 the two readings could not be told apart. Simulating the next build (`LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION = 2`) against copies of real ledgers: AIKit's own ledger and `tally`'s were refused on read, `save_ledger` refused a v1 ledger on write, and `migrate_ledger_schema` was called zero times — the upgrade path could never run. The refusal is safe (the file stays untouched and the message is clear), so the failure mode is every ledger command stopping until the code is fixed, not data loss. Its reach is every ledger in existence: **27, all version 1** — AIKit's plus 26 project ledgers. ADR-174 put it at "all 20 registered projects", which undercounts; that figure is corrected here because past ADRs are not edited (PRINCIPLE-016 R3). ADR-174 reported this defect and left it unfixed under PRINCIPLE-007 R4; this ADR closes it.
- **Decision**:
  1. One predicate, `ledger_version_supported(version)`, answers for both paths: an `int` from 1 to `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The checks used to be two separate `!=` expressions, which is how they came to contradict the documentation together.
  2. `migrate_ledger_schema` stamps the current version on a ledger whose version is missing or an older supported one, so a loaded ledger always declares the format this build writes. A future schema adds its upgrade steps before that stamp. Both callers check the version first, so a newer version never reaches it and is never relabelled.
  3. `save_ledger` upgrades an older supported ledger through `migrate_ledger_schema` before writing, so a file never declares a version older than the format it holds.
  4. Every existing refusal is kept: `0`, `-1`, `True`, `"1"`/`"2"`, `1.0`/`2.0` and any newer version are refused in place on both paths. `test_invalid_ledger_versions_are_refused` is unchanged.
- **Consequences**:
  - *Positive*: Raising `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION` no longer bricks all 27 ledgers; it upgrades them. The code now says what the documentation and PRINCIPLE-013 R4 already said, and the read and write paths cannot disagree again because they share one predicate.
  - *Trade-offs*: None today. With `LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`, "supported" means exactly 1, so behaviour is identical: all 27 real ledgers were loaded after the change and still declare version 1 with their files byte-identical. The new branches are exercised only by tests that patch the constant to 2.
  - *Limitation*: This makes an upgrade *possible*, not automatic. There is no version 2 yet, so no v1-to-v2 transformation exists; the build that raises the version must add its upgrade steps to `migrate_ledger_schema` before the stamp, or it will relabel v1-shaped data as v2.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The change brings the code into line with PRINCIPLE-013 R4 as written and with `knowledge/data_models.md` (PRINCIPLE-016 R5), keeps refusals in place without quarantine (PRINCIPLE-013 R4), and carries failing-first tests for the read and write upgrades plus a guard that every refusal survives (PRINCIPLE-014 R1).
ADR

All three are fixed in three separate commits. Each one passes every gate when checked on its own, and each has an up-to-date codebase map (unlike the other AI's commits). Nothing is pushed.

| Commit | Fix | How I confirmed it |
|---|---|---|

A real contract violation still gets the full revert/abort advice. |
| `9cad254` | Removed the dead fallback in the reachability check and corrected its comment | Added a test that passes on the strict check and fails on a version "repaired" to do what the old comment said. The live check still passes. |
| `2f754e9` | Read and write share one version check: an older valid ledger is upgraded instead of refused | All 27 real ledgers still load as version 1, files byte-identical, so nothing changes today. Every existing refusal still holds. ADR-178 also corrects ADR-174's "20 projects" to 27. |

Two mistakes of mine came up along the way:
- **A failed checkpoint went unnoticed.** I piped commands through `tail`, so `&&` checked `tail`'s exit code and missed a failure. I re-recorded it; the ledger is correct now.
- **My handoff format can't hold `;` inside a value**, because `;` separates the fields. The error names the problem clearly, but it's a real limit of the ADR-174 format.

## The flaky test: found, and it needs your decision

The cause is dogfood's startup check. It times `aikit.py --help` once against a 200 ms limit. That command takes at least ~160 ms on this machine, because it loads almost every module just to print help. Normal timing noise on Windows pushes it over 200 ms in about 16% of runs.

- **It's older than this session.** Every revision I measured back to 10-22 morning shows it. The command joined this check on 10-17 (ADR-119). The 47–71 ms figure in `dogfood.py`'s comment predates that, so it isn't a slowdown.
- **It's frequent.** One full Phase 4 run triggers the check up to three times, through the test suite, `check_test_budgets.py` and `dogfood.py`. It failed 2 of 4 full runs I recorded, and once while I was verifying `9cad254` by itself (3 of 3 re-runs passed).
- **Two of my earlier explanations were wrong.** I first blamed stray worktrees, then a stale Python cache; both were disproved. I also reported that the environment added ~67 ms, but those runs used `python -I`, under which `aikit.py` crashes on startup, so they timed the crash. The trend table measured the same way was retimed with plain `python`.

I re-ran a failing check whenever I had evidence it was this flake. That's honest only because I wrote it down in each commit message. Doing it routinely would amount to ignoring the gate, so this needs a fix:

1. **Time each command three times and keep the fastest.** The 200 ms limit stays, but it measures how fast the command can start, not one noisy sample. It's a small change, but it is a change to how a gate measures, which is why it's your call.
2. **Make `aikit.py --help` load modules only when a command needs them.** This is the real fix and would likely cut 50+ ms, but it means restructuring `aikit_cli.py`.
3. **Raise the 200 ms limit.** I'd advise against it: it weakens the P-010 rule to hide the problem.

I'd do 1 now and 2 as its own task. Which do you want? And should I push these three commits?

### ADR-179: The `--help` Cold-Start Budget Is 250ms
- **Date**: 2026-10-23
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: PRINCIPLE-010 R5 required every CLI to answer `--help` in under 200ms as a fresh process, and `scripts/dogfood.py` checked it with one timed run per entrypoint. `aikit.py` joined that loop with ADR-119; it imports nearly every module to print help, and on the development machine it has a floor of about 155-160ms (25 live samples: median 175ms, p90 217ms, 4 over 200ms). Every other entrypoint stays under 145ms even at its worst. A single sample therefore failed on ordinary Windows process-start jitter: the dogfood track failed in 2 of 4 full Phase 4 sequences, surfaced through three gates at once (the suite's `test_dogfood_run_passes_every_track`, `check_test_budgets.py`, which runs the suite, and `dogfood.py` itself), and once in an isolated `verify_commit.py` run that passed on three re-runs. Measuring every revision back to 10-22 showed the same floor, so no commit caused it. The comment beside `budget_ms` cited medians of 47-71ms from ADR-083, which predate `aikit.py` joining the loop. Three options were put to the user: time each entrypoint best-of-three under the same 200ms, make `aikit.py --help` import lazily, or raise the budget. The user chose to raise it to 250ms.
- **Decision**:
  1. PRINCIPLE-010's capsule and R5 state `--help` under 250ms; `scripts/dogfood.py` checks `budget_ms = 250`; the README command matrix says the same. All eight Tier 1 targets are regenerated; the capsule's length is unchanged, so the Tier 1 budget is unaffected.
  2. R2's separate 200ms threshold ("threads only for steps >=200ms") is a different rule about concurrency and is unchanged.
  3. The `budget_ms` comment now records the measured floor and why ADR-083's medians no longer describe the loop.
  4. `TestRewrittenPrincipleWording.test_rewritten_principles_have_one_reading` pins PRINCIPLE-010's rule text, so its two `--help` phrases change from 200ms to 250ms. That is a rule-text pin following a rule the user changed, not a weakened behavioural assertion; it is named here under PRINCIPLE-014 R3. `TestRuleNumberParity` continues to tie the rule text to dogfood's constant.
- **Consequences**:
  - *Positive*: A red startup track again signals a real slowdown rather than an unlucky sample. Idle, 80 consecutive `aikit.py --help` runs: median 158ms, p95 180ms, worst 204ms, none over 250ms.
  - *Trade-offs*: The rule is looser by 50ms for every CLI, including the five that never needed it. The underlying cause is untouched: `aikit.py` still imports nearly every module to print help, and its ~160ms floor now has about 90ms of margin instead of 40ms. A slowdown in that import chain is now 50ms later to be caught.
  - *Not done*: lazy imports in `aikit_cli.py`, which would lower the floor itself, and best-of-three timing in `dogfood.py`, which would remove the single-sample noise. Either remains available and neither conflicts with this budget.
- Cross-principle check: PRINCIPLE-010 R5 changed (the `--help` budget); R2's concurrency threshold did not. Against the principles that cite PRINCIPLE-010: PRINCIPLE-007 (no conflict; no TODO or stub, and the change stays inside the user's decision), PRINCIPLE-009 (no conflict; no module structure changed), PRINCIPLE-011 (no conflict; its exit 0/1/2 contract and `--help` behaviour are unchanged, only the time limit moved), PRINCIPLE-013 (no conflict; no persisted state), PRINCIPLE-014 (served: the pin and parity tests encode the new number, and the edited pin is named above), PRINCIPLE-018 (no conflict; dogfood remains a pre-commit gate with a now-reliable signal).
ADR

def find_phantom_keys(files: List[Path]) -> List[Tuple[str, str]]:
    """State keys read by production code that no production code ever writes."""
    # Strict by design: a read key needs a producer the AST can see - a dict-literal key or a
    # subscript assignment - or an entry in EXTERNAL_SCHEMA_KEYS for data another program writes.
    # A key written only through a comprehension or a loop over a tuple of names is flagged even
    # if its name appears as a literal elsewhere; write such keys literally instead.
    #
    # A fallback here once meant to excuse any key appearing more than once as a literal. It
    # collected those literals into a set, so its count never exceeded 1 and it never excused
    # anything. It was removed rather than repaired: repaired, it would have passed the hidden
    # producer this shield caught in the ADR-174 handoff work (`test_a_producer_hidden_in_a_
    # comprehension_is_flagged` pins this).
    reads, writes = collect_state_keys(files)
    return [(key, module) for key, module in sorted(reads.items())

The review turned up two small gaps in my own commits. I fixed both, checked every commit, and pushed: `9653975..7b7412d` is on origin as a plain fast-forward, and origin now matches local.

## What the review found

| Commit | Verdict | What I checked |
|---|---|---|
| `0a34821` ui finish message | ✅ Sound | The review-only branch triggers only when *every* finding is `ui.review-missing`, and only `finish()` produces that one. Any other finding, even an unrecognised one, gets the full contract advice. |
| `9cad254` dead fallback removed | ⚠️ Comment flaw → fixed | The comment split the protecting test's name across two lines. Searching for the test never found the comment explaining why the fallback must not come back. |
| `2f754e9` ledger version | ⚠️ Gap → fixed | I made a build read versions 1 to N but left the error saying it "reads version N". That's correct today, but wrong on the exact version bump this commit prepares for. No third version check exists; `_refuse_newer_ledger_on_disk` goes through the shared one. |
| `16deb22` 250 ms limit | ✅ Sound | Every `--help` mention was updated. The one remaining "<200ms" is in `principles_audit_ledger.md`, which the README marks as a snapshot taken at ADR-107, so it should stay as written. |

**Fixes:**
- **`9642c31`** puts the test name on one line, so searching for it finds both the test and the comment.
- **`7b7412d`** changes the error to name the full range ("reads versions 1 to 2") once a build reads more than one version. While only version 1 exists, the text is identical to before: I compared it with the previous version for five different invalid values. A new test checks both the old and new wording.

**Before pushing:**
- All six unpushed commits passed every gate one at a time.
- Each one's codebase map matched its code — the other AI's commits had failed this.
- A credential scan of exactly the commits being pushed came back clean. GitHub's push protection is what forced the other AI to rewrite history.
- Origin hadn't moved since I last fetched, so this was a fast-forward, not a force-push.

## Older problems I noticed, not touched

None of these is in the pushed commits; tell me if you want any of them fixed:
- **Reachability check:** it counts `.setdefault("k", ...)` only as a read, even though it can create the key. A key that is only ever created that way would be wrongly flagged as missing its writer. Nothing in the repo does this today.
- **Ledger version error text:** for invalid values like `0` or `True`, the error blames "a different AIKit whose format this build does not understand". The real problem there is a bad value, not a different AIKit.
- **Slow `aikit.py --help`:** it still takes about 160 ms just to start. ADR-179 records two ways to bring that down.
- **Leftover worktrees:** the two stale ones in your Temp folder are still there and safe to delete; leave Kilo's.
Fix. /goal Then analyze last 5 push. Verify and analyze them for bugs, fixes, gaps and improvements.

Two parts: fix the four items, then review the last five pushes. Starting with the one change outside the repo: the stale worktrees. Before deleting anything I'll check that neither holds uncommitted work.

class TestAikitHelpFastPath(unittest.TestCase):
    """
    `python aikit.py --help` parses with scripts/aikit_parser.py alone, so it must stay light
    and agree with the modules it mirrors instead of importing them (ADR-180).
    """

    def test_parser_constants_match_the_modules_they_mirror(self):
        import scripts.aikit_parser as grammar
        import scripts.disruption_recovery as ledger
        self.assertEqual(grammar.ROOT_DIR, ledger.ROOT_DIR)
        self.assertEqual(grammar.TEMP_STALE_SECONDS, ledger.TEMP_STALE_SECONDS)

    def test_parser_module_imports_only_the_standard_library_at_top_level(self):
        # One AIKit import here would make every `--help` load the whole graph again, silently.
        tree = ast.parse((ROOT_DIR / "scripts" / "aikit_parser.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        top = [node for node in tree.body if isinstance(node, (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom))]
        names = [alias.name for node in top if isinstance(node, ast.Import) for alias in node.names]
        names += [node.module for node in top if isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom)]
        self.assertTrue(names, "expected the parser module to import argparse at least")
        self.assertEqual([name for name in names if name.split(".")[0] == "scripts"], [])

    def test_cli_reexports_the_parser_so_existing_callers_keep_working(self):
        import scripts.aikit_cli as cli
        import scripts.aikit_parser as grammar
        self.assertIs(cli.build_parser, grammar.build_parser)
        self.assertIs(cli.report_error, grammar.report_error)

### ADR-180: `aikit.py --help` Parses With the Grammar Alone
- **Date**: 2026-10-23
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: `aikit.py` imported `scripts/aikit_cli.py` before parsing anything, and `aikit_cli` imports every module the commands use (`disruption_recovery`, `project_registry`, `project_publish`, `subagent_delegate`, `ui_contract`, `update_knowledge_base`, and through them `check_secrets` and `dataclasses`). Printing help therefore cost the whole graph: about 158ms minimum and 165ms median on the development machine, the reason ADR-179 raised the `--help` budget to 250ms. PRINCIPLE-010 R5 already asks a CLI to import only the standard library at top level and anything else after argument dispatch. `-X importtime` showed no single hog (each first-party module costs 2-3ms of self time), so only not loading the command layer could help. `build_parser` needed just `argparse`, `Path`, its own `TriadArgumentParser`, `ROOT_DIR` and `TEMP_STALE_SECONDS`.
- **Decision**:
  1. `report_error`, `TriadArgumentParser` and `build_parser` move verbatim, by line range rather than retyping, to `scripts/aikit_parser.py`, which imports only the standard library at top level. `ProjectError` is imported inside `TriadArgumentParser.error`, the one path that raises it, and under `TYPE_CHECKING` for the annotation. `aikit_parser` never imports `aikit_cli`, so the import-cycle audit, which also counts imports inside functions, stays green.
  2. `aikit_cli` re-exports the three names, so `from scripts.aikit_cli import build_parser` and every one of the 66 test patches on `scripts.aikit_cli` keep working unchanged.
  3. `aikit.py` parses with `aikit_parser` alone when `-h` or `--help` appears in its arguments; help and usage errors exit there. Any command line that gets past that parse falls through to `aikit_cli.main`, which parses it again, so the outcome is the same either way.
  4. `aikit_parser` mirrors `ROOT_DIR` (the same `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent` nine other modules already define) and `TEMP_STALE_SECONDS = 60` instead of importing `disruption_recovery`. A unit test pins both to the originals, another fails if `aikit_parser` gains a top-level `scripts` import, and an integration test checks under `-X importtime` that `--help` never loads `scripts.aikit_cli` while a real command still does.
- **Consequences**:
  - *Positive*: 50 help and usage-error forms of `aikit.py` (top level, every subcommand with `-h` and `--help`, every `ui` action, and malformed lines such as `bogus --help`, `checkpoint app --desc -h` and `-- --help`) were captured before the change and after: exit code, stdout and stderr all byte-identical. `aikit.py --help` now measures 123ms minimum and 133ms median (40 runs), down from about 158 and 165.
  - *Trade-offs*: The saving is about 35ms, not the roughly 80ms first projected. The projection compared against a process that only imported `argparse`, but the remaining cost is Python 3.14's own `argparse` pulling in `dataclasses`, `inspect`, `_colorize` and `shutil` (about 35ms), plus constructing a 14-command parser (about 45ms). Going further would mean building only the subparser a given help screen needs, which is more machinery than the gain justifies. `ROOT_DIR` and `TEMP_STALE_SECONDS` now each have one more definition, guarded by the parity test. A help request is parsed twice when it reaches `main`, which happens only for a line where `-h` is not actually the help option, such as after `--`.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The change brings `aikit.py`'s help path in line with PRINCIPLE-010 R5's top-level-import clause, keeps PRINCIPLE-011 R5's exit codes and output byte-identical, adds no import cycle (PRINCIPLE-009 R5), lists the new module in the README tree in the same commit (PRINCIPLE-005 R2, R5), and carries failing-first tests (PRINCIPLE-014 R1).
ADR

### ADR-181: Annotations Must Resolve on Every Supported Python
- **Date**: 2026-10-23
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: Commit e18a1b3 (ADR-172) annotated `project_is_clean` and `project_payload` in `scripts/aikit_cli.py` with `Dict` without importing it. Python 3.14, the only interpreter on the development machine, evaluates annotations only when they are read (PEP 649), so every local test and gate passed. Python 3.10 to 3.13, which the README states as supported and CI is configured to test, evaluate annotations when `def` runs, so importing `scripts.aikit_cli` raises `NameError` and every `aikit.py` command fails. The defect reached origin in push 9653975 and stayed there. CI caught nothing because it ran nothing: every GitHub Actions job since at least 2026-10-19 reports "The job was not started because your account is locked due to a billing issue", with zero steps executed, so the Python 3.10/3.13 and Ubuntu legs the CI workflow exists for have verified no push in that time. Two of the three ways a 3.10 floor can be broken on a newer interpreter were already guarded locally: syntax, by the AST gate parsing with `feature_version=MIN_PYTHON`, and standard-library APIs, by `test_no_standard_library_apis_newer_than_the_minimum`. Deferred annotation evaluation was not.
- **Decision**:
  1. `scripts/aikit_cli.py` imports `Dict`.
  2. `TestAnnotationsResolveOnEverySupportedPython.test_every_annotation_in_scripts_names_something_defined` imports every module in `scripts/` and reads the `__annotations__` of every function, class and method defined there. Reading them forces evaluation on Python 3.14, reproducing what 3.10 to 3.13 do at definition time; on those versions an undefined name already fails the import. It runs in the unit tier, without spawning a process, in about 6ms. Before the fix it reported exactly the two `Dict` annotations and nothing else.
- **Consequences**:
  - *Positive*: `aikit.py` imports again on every supported Python, and the whole class of deferred-annotation `NameError` is caught locally on any interpreter, which matters most while CI cannot run.
  - *Limitation*: This was verified by simulation, not on a real Python 3.10 or 3.13, because none is installed and CI is down. The guard covers annotations on module-level functions, classes and their methods; an annotation on a nested function would escape it, though none exists today. Runtime differences outside syntax, standard-library names and annotations are still unchecked until CI runs again.
  - *Requires the user*: GitHub Actions stays inert until the account's billing lock is resolved in GitHub's billing settings; nothing in this repository can restart it.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The change serves PRINCIPLE-003 R4 (platform and version parity, here the README's Python 3.10 floor), PRINCIPLE-011 (clone-and-run: every documented command imports again on the stated minimum) and PRINCIPLE-014 R1 (a failing-first test that reproduced the defect).

def terminate_process_tree(proc: "subprocess.Popen") -> None:
    """
    Kill a process and all of its children (PRINCIPLE-015 Rule 2).

    A plain `proc.kill()` orphans grandchildren, which is how dogfood runs leak zombies and
    collide on ports. Windows has no process groups, so the tree is torn down with
    `taskkill /F /T`; POSIX kills the whole process group with SIGKILL.
    """
    if proc.poll() is not None:
        return
    try:
        if sys.platform == "win32":
            subprocess.run(
                ["taskkill", "/F", "/T", "/PID", str(proc.pid)],
                capture_output=True, timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT,
            )
        else:
            os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), signal.SIGKILL)
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        # Last resort: at least kill the direct child rather than leaving it running.
        try:
            proc.kill()
        except OSError:  # hygiene: allow the child is already gone; the tree teardown continues
            pass
    finally:
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:  # hygiene: allow the process was killed; waiting longer cannot help

  2. When commit delivery is not authorized, the agent stops after Phase 4 and reports the uncommitted files instead of committing.

content.text:
The fixes are done and verified, and the five-push review found **two critical problems** — one of them a regression I introduced.

## Part 1 — Fixes (four commits, each verified alone, not yet pushed)

| Commit | What | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `f099d8b` | The reachability check now treats `.setdefault("k", …)` as creating the key, not just reading it | Failing-first test; the strict comprehension test still passes |
| `92d28df` | An invalid ledger version (`0`, `True`, `"2"`…) gets its own message instead of blaming "a different AIKit" | Newer-version text kept identical |
| `61f1254` | `aikit.py --help` builds only the parser (new `scripts/aikit_parser.py`) instead of importing every module | **All 50 help and usage-error outputs byte-identical.** Startup minimum 158→123 ms, median 165→133 ms |
| `a0e310d` | **Restores the missing `Dict` import** (found along the way; see below) | A new test catches the whole class of bug |

Removed the two stale Temp worktrees after confirming they were clean; Kilo's is untouched.

Corrections to what I told you before:
- I projected `--help` would halve to ~80 ms. Real saving is ~35 ms, because Python 3.14's `argparse` (~35 ms) and building a 14-command parser (~45 ms) can't be skipped.
- The README check finds `aikit.py`'s commands by reading `aikit_cli.py`'s source text, which I missed when I moved the parser. Phase 4 caught it and the check now reads `aikit_parser.py`.

## Part 2 — The last five pushes (25 commits, ~6,300 lines)

**🔴 1. CI has not run in at least five days.** Every job since 10-19 says: *"The job was not started because your account is locked due to a billing issue."* Zero steps ran, so no push in this window was tested on Python 3.10/3.13 or Ubuntu. Only you can fix this, in GitHub's billing settings.

**🔴 2. `aikit.py` on origin crashes on Python 3.10–3.13 — I caused it.** In `e18a1b3` I used `Dict` in two type hints without importing it. Python 3.14, the only version on this machine, doesn't evaluate type hints until they're read, so every local test passed. 3.10–3.13, the versions the README supports, evaluate them at import, so **every command fails**. Both of the last two pushes carry it, and origin stays broken until `a0e310d` is pushed. The new test forces type hints to be evaluated the old way, completing local 3.10 coverage alongside the existing syntax and library-name checks. It's verified by simulation only, since no 3.10 or 3.13 is installed.

**🟠 3. `aikit check` pushes to GitHub by default, and no document says so.** The runbook tells agents to run it as a project's Phase 4, yet once its checks pass it pushes unpushed commits unless given `--no-push`, which no document mentions. An agent on a host that may push only when asked would publish without permission, against P-018 R4. The push dates from 10-17; push 4 added the "push only when authorized" rule without changing this command.

**🟠 4. `check_secrets --all` skips every file with a non-ASCII name, without saying so.** I committed the same fake token in `ascii_notes.txt` and `şifre_notları.txt`: one finding, no warning. Git quotes such names (`"\305\237ifre…txt"`), the scanner sees a `.txt"` extension, and drops the file — breaking its own rule that a skipped file must never read as clean. The pre-commit scan and the publish scan read file *contents* from git diffs, so they still catch it, just without naming the file. Present since the scanner was written on 10-16.

**🟠 5. On Windows, a multi-line command silently runs only its first line.** I tested `"exit 0\nexit 7"` through the project command runner: exit **0**. On Linux/macOS it returns 7. A project test command or UI proof command with a line break would pass on Windows while skipping its later steps. Present since 10-17; push 4 extended it to UI proof commands.

**🟡 Smaller:**
- **Stale codebase maps.** I checked every recorded file size in all 25 commits: only the five from the other AI's history rewrite are stale. They're published, so fixing them would need a force-push; the latest commit is correct, so I'd leave them.
- **Time limits keep rising.** Three were raised in five pushes: integration tests 250→350 ms per test, unit tests 8→10 ms, and `--help` 200→250 ms. The integration average went from ~216 to ~280 ms in this session alone, now 80% of its ceiling.
- **A check that can switch itself off.** If the parser file is ever renamed, the README's command check silently stops running.

**✅ What checked out:** the 7 commits in pushes 3–4 each pass every gate on their own. The 4 in push 5 pass all their tests but miss that period's 250 ms test-time limit when re-run today; ADR-164 records the machine exceeding it at the time. The code that runs project commands is solid: it kills the whole process tree, has timeouts, closes stdin and handles UTF-8. The AGPL license switch is consistent throughout.

## What needs you

class TestSecretScanSeesNonAsciiPaths(unittest.TestCase):
    """
    git quotes a non-ASCII path ("\\305\\237ifre.txt") unless told otherwise, so `--all` read a
    `.txt"` suffix and skipped the file silently, and diff findings lost their file name (ADR-182).
    """

    # Built at run time so no credential-shaped literal sits in this source file.
    GITHUB = "ghp_" + "REDACTED"
    GITLAB = "glpat-" + "aB3dE5gH7jK9mN1pQ3rS"
    TURKISH = "şifre_notları.txt"

    def make_repo(self) -> Path:
        repo = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="test_qpath_"))
        self.addCleanup(remove_tree, repo)
        for args in (["init", "-q"], ["config", "user.name", "t"],
                     ["config", "user.email", "t@example.invalid"]):
            subprocess.run(["git", *args], cwd=repo, check=True, timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT)
        return repo

    def scan(self, repo: Path, mode: str) -> str:
        res = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT_DIR / "scripts" / "check_secrets.py"),
                              mode, "--workspace", str(repo)],
                             capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace",
                             timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL)
        self.assertEqual(res.returncode, 1, res.stdout[-600:])
        return res.stdout

    def test_all_scans_a_tracked_file_whose_name_is_not_ascii(self):
        repo = self.make_repo()
        (repo / "notes.txt").write_text(f'token = "{self.GITHUB}"\n', encoding="utf-8")
        (repo / self.TURKISH).write_text(f'token = "{self.GITHUB}"\n', encoding="utf-8")
        subprocess.run(["git", "add", "-A"], cwd=repo, check=True, timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT)
        subprocess.run(["git", "commit", "-qm", "init"], cwd=repo, check=True, timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT)
        out = self.scan(repo, "--all")
        self.assertIn("2 potential secret", out, "the non-ASCII file was skipped")
        self.assertIn(self.TURKISH, out)

    def test_staged_findings_name_a_non_ascii_file(self):
        repo = self.make_repo()
        (repo / self.TURKISH).write_text(f'key = "{self.GITLAB}"\n', encoding="utf-8")
        subprocess.run(["git", "add", "-A"], cwd=repo, check=True, timeout=PROC_TIMEOUT)
        out = self.scan(repo, "--staged")
        self.assertIn(f"{self.TURKISH}:1", out, "the finding lost its file name")
